title: Divination Moon Blocks (Jiaobei)
summary: A pair of crescent-shaped red blocks, clasped in your palms and dropped to the floor -- this is jiaobei, the most direct way Taiwanese people put a question to the gods. Three possible answers -- holy, laughing, and negative blocks -- and this guide shows you how to ask, and how to read the deity's reply.
content:
Kneeling before the altar with something weighing on your mind, the pair of crescent-shaped red blocks in your hands becomes your direct line to the deity. These half-moon wooden blocks -- jiaobei, or divination moon blocks -- let worshippers hold a simple "yes or no" conversation with the gods. Taiwanese people have been doing this for centuries, and it remains one of the most everyday sights in any temple.

【Shape and Material】
A pair of blocks: one side flat (the yang side), one side rounded (the yin side). Most are carved from wood or bamboo, though some temples use plastic. The more particular temples choose fine woods like sandalwood or camphor, consecrated through a blessing ceremony before they can truly "reach" the deity.

【Getting Ready】
Don't rush to throw. First raise the blocks above the main incense burner and circle them clockwise three times -- this is called "passing over the censer," letting the blocks soak up the energy of the incense smoke. Only after this purification do they gain the power to communicate. Some worshippers cup the blocks between their palms and rub them gently, like greeting the deity.

【Stating Your Case and Asking】
Kneeling or standing, the first thing you do is report your "name and details": your full name, lunar birthday, and home address, so the deity knows who is asking. Your question must be a yes-or-no one -- "This humble devotee asks: is this job right for me?" Make it clear and specific, never vague, and ask only one thing at a time.

【How to Cast】
Cup the blocks at chest height with both hands, then let them drop naturally and bounce on the floor. Don't hurl them down hard -- the deity wants sincerity, not force.

【Reading the Answer】
- Holy block (sheng jiao, one flat and one raised): the deity nods -- yes, agreed. Usually three holy blocks in a row are needed to count. For major matters like dividing a deity's spirit to a new temple or building one, you may need seven or even twelve consecutive holy blocks before the deity gives way.
- Laughing block (xiao jiao, both flat sides up): both faces up, as if the deity is smiling but not answering. Perhaps your question wasn't clear enough, the timing isn't right, or the deity finds it a little amusing. Rethink it and cast again.
- Negative block (yin jiao, both rounded sides up): both faces down -- the deity shakes its head. No. Don't stubbornly keep asking the same thing; approach it from another angle, or come back another day.

【Standing Block (A Miracle)】
Every so often, the whole temple holds its breath: a block lands and stands upright without toppling. This is a "standing block," rare enough to be counted a miracle, usually meaning the deity has something especially important to say. If it happens, don't interpret it yourself -- ask temple staff for help, and you may need to draw a fortune stick to understand the message fully.

【Things to Remember】
- Don't cast more than three times for the same question; asking too often is seen as disrespecting the deity's will.
- Always offer incense and state your case before casting -- otherwise those blocks are just two ordinary pieces of wood with no power at all.
- Once you've received the deity's answer, step forward and bow three times in thanks.
- Some temples now offer "online jiaobei" apps, but most older devotees still believe the block you cast in person, standing before the deity, is the one that truly works.

title: Jigai: Ritual for Reversing Bad Fortune
summary: When your luck keeps sliding, everything goes wrong, and your health won't settle, Taiwanese people head to the temple for jigai -- also called bu yun, or fortune-mending. Through a ritual master's ceremony, your misfortune is transferred onto a substitute effigy and burned away, symbolizing that the old bad luck has left and new fortune has arrived.
content:
Lately nothing seems to go right -- you feel listless, sleep badly, and can't put your finger on what's wrong. An elder might tell you, "Go and mend your luck." That is jigai (also called bu yun, or fortune restoration), the ritual Taiwanese turn to in a low patch to ask the gods to drive off calamity and dissolve misfortune -- and people still rely on it today.

【What Is Jigai?】
"Ji" means to make an offering; "gai" means to change one's fortune. When someone's luck sinks, their health falters, or they've offended some baleful influence, they can ask a Taoist priest or ritual master at the temple to step in. Using a "substitute" -- a straw figure, a paper effigy, or a paper horse-and-carriage -- the practitioner draws the bad luck and negative energy off the person and onto the stand-in, then reports to the deity to petition for resolution. The old misfortune departs with the substitute, so new fortune has room to come in.

【Common Occasions】
- When you clash with the year's Tai Sui (the Grand Duke Jupiter), when your luck stalls, or when setbacks keep piling up.
- After a fright, or when you feel spiritually unsettled -- the simplest form of jigai is shoujing (fright-calming), which volunteers at many temples can perform, Xingtian Temple being the most famous.
- During a long illness, or when accidents come one after another.
- When you hit a metaphysical "life gate" (guansha), such as a "vehicle gate" or "water gate."
- When a child cries endlessly at night or is easily startled.

【The Ritual】
Before you go, prepare your Eight Characters birth data (the lunar year, month, day, and hour of birth) and a piece of clothing worn close to the body to represent you. The ritual master first reports to the deity, then works with incantations, talismans, and ritual implements. The substitute is inscribed with your name and birth data, and over the ceremony your ill luck and negative energy are "transferred" onto it piece by piece -- until it is finally burned, and the misfortune scatters with the smoke. When it's done, you receive a peace talisman, a red string, or a fire-blessed purification charm, a sign that a deity now watches over you and your fortune has been reset.

【Shoujing: Fright-Calming】
Shoujing is the best-known simple form of jigai. After a car accident, a fall, or a nightmare, when a person turns restless, loses their appetite, and can't sleep soundly, they can go to a temple for shoujing. The practitioner holds a stick of incense or a handful of rice, softly reciting incantations while facing the person, and calls the scattered soul back bit by bit. The shoujing performed by the volunteer "service workers" at Xingtian Temple is the most renowned of all -- even people who aren't especially devout will go and line up when something feels off inside.

【Cost and a Reminder】
At most temples shoujing is free, or given by voluntary donation. A formal jigai ceremony varies by temple, from a few hundred to a few thousand NT dollars. One reminder: jigai is about finding peace of mind. If your body is genuinely unwell, still see a doctor -- letting faith and medicine work side by side is the wisest thing you can do for yourself.

title: Taoist Liturgical Ceremonies (Keyi)
summary: Gongs, suona, and cymbals sound together as a Taoist priest in a bagua-patterned robe shakes the Emperor Bell and paces the steps of the Big Dipper -- this is "doing fashi," also called keyi, the Taoist liturgical ceremony. From birth to death, trained priests use a rigorous set of rites to bless people, dispel calamity, and bridge the human and spirit worlds.
content:
Gongs, suona, and cymbals strike up at once. A Taoist priest in a robe embroidered with the eight trigrams shakes the Emperor Bell in one hand while his feet trace the seven stars of the Big Dipper across the ground -- one of the most theatrical sights on any temple plaza in Taiwan: doing fashi, also known as keyi (Taoist liturgy). Presided over by professionally trained priests, it is a bridge between the human world and the realm of spirits, present at every threshold of life from birth to death.

【What Is a Liturgical Ceremony?】
Fashi is not something you can perform at home. The priest leading it must be professionally trained, reaching the deities step by step through chanting scripture, reciting incantations, "bugang tadou" (a ritual gait symbolizing treading upon the stars of the Big Dipper), and "cunxiang" (inwardly visualizing the deities descending). It takes years of cultivation and religious knowledge -- not something an ordinary worshipper can do alone.

【Common Types of Ceremony】
- Blessing rites: Tai Sui pacification, lighting bright lamps, fortune restoration, and peace-prayer assemblies -- to pray for a smooth, safe year ahead and to ward off calamity, usually held around the first lunar month or during a temple's major celebrations.
- Salvation rites: Ghost Month universal salvation (Zhongyuan Pudu), memorial rites for the dead, and merit assemblies -- accumulating merit for departed relatives or wandering souls to help them escape suffering, the most important religious activity of the seventh lunar month.
- Exorcism rites: house-cleansing, shoujing (fright-calming), and driving off evil. When a home is unsettled, family members fall ill one after another, or strange things happen, a ritual master may be invited to the house to perform them.
- Thanksgiving rites: ceremonies to repay the gods after a wish comes true; and the jiao ritual (a community-wide peace ceremony), a grand, large-scale event usually held only once every three to five years.
- Funerary rites: merit-making for the dead, soul-guiding, coffin-sealing, and burial ceremonies. Taoist liturgy plays a heavy role in Taiwanese funerals, guiding the departed soul all the way to the next world.

【The Scene and the Implements】
An altar is raised at the ceremony site, set with images of the Celestial Worthies, command flags, and talismans. The color of the priest's robe carries meaning -- red for blessing rites, black for salvation rites. Each implement has its job: the Emperor Bell is shaken to summon the deities, the wooden fish keeps the rhythm of the chanting, the dragon horn is blown to intimidate evil spirits, the treasure sword slays demons, and a wave of the command flag issues divine orders. At the back, musicians accompany on gongs, drums, suona (Chinese oboe), and cymbals -- music at once solemn and full of dramatic tension, one of the most distinctive strands of Taiwanese religious music.

【Cost and Choosing a Master】
The cost varies enormously: from a small shoujing (free to a few hundred NT dollars) all the way to a grand jiao ritual (hundreds of thousands to millions). When choosing a ritual master, favor those recommended by reputable temples or with a good word-of-mouth reputation -- and steer clear of dubious "itinerant practitioners" of unknown origin.

title: Talismans and Protective Charms (Fulu)
summary: The little red pouch tucked in a wallet, the folded yellow-paper bagua hanging from a scooter key -- these are fulu, or peace talismans, the most personal form of protection in Taiwanese folk belief. Requested at a temple and "passed over the censer," they are carried close to keep the bearer safe and turn misfortune aside.
content:
Open most Taiwanese people's wallets and you'll likely find a slip of yellow paper, folded small and slipped into a red plastic sleeve -- a peace talisman. From the ping'an fu handed out at temples to the house-guarding charms drawn by a Taoist priest, fulu (also called fu or shenfu) have passed through nearly every household in Taiwan, quietly watching over the family's daily life.

【Meaning and How It Works】
A talisman writes a deity's spiritual power -- in special characters, symbols, and figures -- onto yellow paper, red paper, or silk. It works like a "decree" or "written order" issued in the deity's own hand, carrying divine authority and protection. But whether a talisman is potent rests on three things: the cultivation of the ritual master who draws it, the deity's blessing, and your own sincere faith. Take away any one, and it loses its power.

【Common Types】
- Peace talisman (ping'an fu): the most common and widely used. A sheet of yellow paper inscribed with sacred symbols, folded into a bagua shape or a rectangle and placed in a red amulet sleeve. After being "passed over the censer" at the main burner (circled clockwise three times), it is carried on the person for safe passage and to turn away bad luck. Nearly every temple offers one -- it is the most basic protective object in Taiwanese practice.
- Purification talisman (jing fu): used after a funeral, a hospital or sickbed visit, or a trip to a cemetery or other unclean place. The talisman is dissolved in clean water, which is then used to wash the face and hands or sprinkled over the body to clear away negative energy and cleanse one's field.
- House-guarding talisman (zhenzhai fu): pasted above the door lintel, on both sides of the main door, or at a spot in the home designated by a ritual master, to guard the dwelling and deflect evil. Common when moving into a new home or when strange things keep happening in the house.
- Wealth talisman (zhaocai fu): requested at wealth-god temples for prosperity, then placed in a wallet, cash register, or safe.
- Marriage talisman (yinyuan fu): requested at a Yue Lao (Matchmaker God) temple to seek a good match.
- Personal protection talisman (fuling): custom-drawn by a Taoist priest from your personal birth chart, offering the most targeted protection.

【The Right Way to Request One】
1. First offer incense before the deity and state your name, birthday, and address.
2. Explain clearly why you are requesting the talisman and what you seek.
3. Cast divination blocks to ask the deity's permission; only proceed once you receive a holy block.
4. Collect the talisman at the service counter or talisman station.
5. Raise it above the main incense burner and circle it clockwise three times -- passing over the censer -- to let it drink in the incense energy and switch on its power.
6. Store it well and carry it, or use it as directed.

【Using and Replacing It】
- A peace talisman is usually replaced once a year. Before Lunar New Year, take the old one to the temple's furnace to be burned, then request a fresh one for the coming year.
- Don't keep a talisman in an unclean spot (for instance, sitting on it in a back pocket) -- that disrespects the deity.
- Replace a talisman promptly once it is damaged, waterlogged, or faded.
- Taking someone else's talisman as your own is taboo; use only the talisman you requested yourself.
- Never toss an old talisman in the trash. Return it to the temple furnace to be burned properly.

title: Pacifying Tai Sui (The Grand Duke Jupiter)
summary: "When Tai Sui sits overhead, if there is no joy there will be disaster" -- in a year when your zodiac sign clashes with Tai Sui, Taiwanese people go to the temple before Lunar New Year to "pacify Tai Sui," handing over their name and birth data for the temple to enshrine the presiding Grand Duke Jupiter and praying for a smooth, safe year.
content:
Around Lunar New Year, the Tai Sui halls of the big temples are always packed with long queues -- people clutching their ID details, waiting to register for "an tai sui." Most of them share one thing in common: this year their zodiac sign clashes with Tai Sui, and they want to get through the year safely, turning misfortune into good fortune.

【What Is Tai Sui?】
The Tai Sui Star Deity governs the fortunes of a given year. "Tai Sui" originally referred to Jupiter, the "Year Star" -- the ancients noticed it takes about twelve years to circle the heavens, matching the twelve Earthly Branches, which grew into a system of sixty Tai Sui star deities taking turns on duty through the sixty-year cycle. Each year one of them presides, ruling that year's fortunes. As the folk saying goes, "When Tai Sui sits overhead, if there is no joy there will be disaster" -- meaning those who offend the year's Tai Sui tend to face a bumpy, obstacle-strewn year.

【Who Needs to Pacify Tai Sui?】
- Direct clash (zhi Tai Sui): your zodiac animal shares the Earthly Branch of the year's Tai Sui. In the Year of the Dragon, for example, those born in a Dragon year are in direct clash.
- Opposing clash (chong Tai Sui): your zodiac animal sits directly opposite the year's Tai Sui. In the Year of the Dragon, those born in a Dog year are in opposing clash.
- Partial clash: some traditions hold that signs in a "punishment," "destruction," or "harm" relationship should also pacify Tai Sui, though temples don't fully agree on the standard.
- Those in a rough patch: even without a clash, anyone who feels nothing is going their way can pacify Tai Sui simply for peace of mind.

【How It's Done】
The old way was to set up a spirit tablet or a strip of red paper bearing the presiding Tai Sui star deity's name on the family altar, offering incense morning and night. But modern life is busy, so most people register at a temple and let it make the offerings on their behalf. The process runs roughly like this:
1. Prepare your details: name, lunar date of birth (year, month, day, and hour), and address.
2. Register at the Tai Sui hall's service counter and pay the fee (it varies by temple, generally a few hundred to a few thousand NT dollars).
3. Temple staff inscribe your name and birth data on a Tai Sui lamp or tablet, enshrined in the Tai Sui hall.
4. Through the year, the temple regularly holds scripture-chanting assemblies to pray for blessings and ward off calamity for everyone registered.
5. At year's end, return to the temple to "thank Tai Sui" for the star deity's protection over the past year.

【When to Register】
Registration usually falls between the first and fifteenth days of the first lunar month (the Lantern Festival), with the ninth day -- the birthday of the Jade Emperor -- being the most popular. Some temples open registration before the New Year, and at renowned temples the Tai Sui lamp slots sell out fast, so book early.

【Popular Temples for Pacifying Tai Sui】
- Songshan Ciyou Temple, Taipei: the Tai Sui slots sell out every year.
- Longshan Temple, Wanhua: combines Tai Sui pacification with the lighting of bright lamps.
- Dajia Jenn Lann Temple, Taichung: the top choice for worshippers in central Taiwan.
- City God temples across the island: the City God oversees the judiciary of the underworld, and Tai Sui pacification falls within his purview.

【After Pacifying Tai Sui】
Pacifying Tai Sui doesn't mean you can rest easy. In a clash year it's best to do more good, avoid quarrels, and stay away from high-risk activities. Folk wisdom also warns against moving house, breaking ground for construction, or marrying in a clash year -- though by modern lights, mindset matters most. In the end, pacifying Tai Sui is about setting the heart at ease and serving as a reminder to tread carefully.

title: Drawing Fortune Sticks (Qiuqian)
summary: Divination blocks only answer "yes" or "no" -- but when you need the deity to say more, you draw a fortune stick. Pull a numbered stick from the bamboo cylinder, confirm it with the blocks, then collect the matching four-line poem: qiuqian is one of the most beloved ways to consult the gods in a Taiwanese temple, and this guide shows you how to draw one and how to read it.
content:
By the end of a session with the divination blocks, the deity can only manage "yes" or "no" -- but when did your worries ever come that simple? This is where fortune sticks take over. Drawing fortune sticks (qiuqian, also called "drawing lots" or "seeking a fortune poem") stands with jiaobei as one of the two great channels of communication between people and the gods -- except that here, the deity's guidance comes wrapped in a poem, deeper and finer than a flat yes or no.

【Types and Structure of Fortune Poems】
Taiwanese temples mainly use a few systems of fortune poems:
- Sixty Jiazi sticks: 60 poems arranged by the Heavenly Stems and Earthly Branches (Jiazi, Yichou, Bingyin, and so on), the most common set in Taiwan. Each is a four-line, seven-character verse, graded as "Great Fortune," "Upper Fortune," "Middle Fortune," "Fair," "Lowest," and the like.
- Guanyin's Hundred Poems (Guanyin Lingqian): 100 poems, more often used in Buddhist temples dedicated to Guanyin.
- Guan Di's Hundred Poems: 100 poems, common at temples of Lord Guan (Guan Yu), their verses often drawing on tales from the Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
- Mazu poems: sets of 60 or 100, exclusive to Mazu temples, some verses touching on safety at sea.
Beyond the main verse, each poem usually comes with a plain-language interpretation, a related story or allusion (such as Lu Mengzheng in poverty or Han Xin fishing), and readings for every area of life -- career, marriage, wealth, health, and more.

【The Right Way to Draw】
1. Offer incense and state your case: first offer incense to the deity, clearly giving your name, lunar birthday, address, and the matter you wish to ask about. Keep the question specific (for example, "This humble devotee asks: is this job right for me?"), not vague.
2. Draw a stick: pull one stick from the bamboo cylinder, or let one leap out on its own. The cylinder holds several dozen numbered bamboo sticks.
3. Confirm with the blocks: don't read the poem right away. First cast divination blocks before the deity and ask, "Is this the stick you mean to give me?" Only three holy blocks in a row confirm it; anything else, and you draw again.
4. Retrieve the poem: once confirmed, note the stick number (say, "Number 23") and take the matching poem slip from the poem cabinet.
5. Interpretation: read it yourself, or take it to the temple's "interpretation desk" for a master or volunteer to explain. Many temples keep dedicated interpreters who read the poem against your specific question.

【Famous Temples for Fortune Sticks】
- Longshan Temple, Wanhua: home to the 100 Guanyin poems; one of the busiest temples for drawing sticks.
- Xingtian Temple: known for its Guan Di sticks and famous shoujing (fright-calming) service, and hugely popular for fortune sticks too.
- Xiahai City God Temple, Taipei: reputed as one of the most effective temples for romance-related sticks, and a magnet for singles.
- Lukang Tianhou Temple: known for its Mazu poems, especially accurate for travel and sea fortune.
- Nankunshen Daitian Temple: its "National Fortune Stick," drawn on the first day of Lunar New Year to foretell Taiwan's fortunes for the whole year, makes national headlines.

【The Art of Interpretation】
Reading a fortune poem is an art, not a science. The same verse can point in completely different directions depending on whether you asked about work or about love. A good interpreter first grasps your situation, then weaves together the poem's allusion, its imagery, and its various fortune readings into a whole. An "upper fortune" poem isn't necessarily all good -- it may hide a caution against getting carried away; a "lowest fortune" poem isn't necessarily all bad -- it may be the very turning point where things start to improve. A fortune poem is the deity's reminder and advice, not an unchangeable verdict, so take it with a calm and even heart.

title: Temple Feng Shui and Folk Geomancy
summary: Why does a temple sit with mountains at its back and water to its front? Why must the front door never face the elevator? From choosing a temple site to where you put the living-room sofa, it all comes down to the same thing -- feng shui, the art of geomancy (kanyu) -- which is about letting the "qi" that flows between heaven and earth move smoothly and gather, and it runs deep in the Taiwanese sense of space.
content:
Why do temples always sit with a mountain at their back and water to their front? Why do the elders insist the sofa must be against a wall, and the head of the bed must never face the door? The answers all lie in one body of knowledge -- feng shui, also called kanyu, the art of geomancy. From siting a temple to laying out a home to orienting a grave, its ideas have seeped into every corner of Taiwanese life.

【The Basic Principle】
At the heart of feng shui is a single word: "qi" -- the natural energy that flows between heaven and earth. Good feng shui means letting that qi move freely and settle where it should. The discipline has two great schools:
- Form School (Luantou): reads the land itself -- the shape of mountains, the run of water -- to judge good and ill fortune, weighing the four celestial animals: Vermilion Bird (front), Black Tortoise (rear), Azure Dragon (left), White Tiger (right). The ideal layout has mountains supporting the rear, water before the front, and hills embracing on both sides.
- Compass School (Liqi): uses a luopan (feng shui compass) to measure direction, combining the eight trigrams, five elements, and the Heavenly Stems and Earthly Branches to reckon auspicious and inauspicious directions, with special attention to a building's orientation and the placement of doors and windows.
In practice, most feng shui masters draw on both schools and weigh things together.

【Temple Feng Shui】
The siting and building of a Taiwanese temple is exacting about feng shui:
- Orientation: which way the temple faces (south, west, and so on) is the most basic consideration. Different deities have different ideal orientations -- Mazu temples often face the sea (to protect seafarers), while Earth God temples usually face farmland.
- Bright Hall: an open expanse (the "bright hall") is wanted in front of the temple, symbolizing the gathering of wealth energy. The large plazas before many old temples are exactly this bright hall.
- Water mouth: the direction of nearby water matters greatly. "Water gathering at the heart of heaven" is the finest configuration -- water converging and circling before the temple before it flows away, a sign that wealth energy does not disperse.
- Dragon vein: the siting of major temples weighs the "dragon vein," the course and rise and fall of the mountain ranges. Beigang Chaotian Temple, for instance, is said to rest on a "golden dragon" vein, which is why its spiritual energy runs especially strong.
- Shigandang and Shanhai Zhen: temples and homes alike often set a "Shigandang" stone tablet or a "Shanhai Zhen" plaque at a doorway or corner to resolve the harmful energy of a road or alley aimed straight at them.

【Home Feng Shui Basics】
Taiwanese people are deeply shaped by feng shui in how they decorate and arrange a home:
- Main door: should not face an elevator, a staircase, or an alley aimed at it (a "road clash"), which can cause "wealth leakage." A screen or an entry cabinet can deflect it.
- Kitchen: the stove should not face the tap directly (a water-fire clash), nor turn its back to the door (no "support behind").
- Bedroom: the head of the bed should not face a mirror (prone to causing fright), should not sit beneath an exposed beam (a sign of "pressure"), and the bed should not face straight at the door.
- Living room: the sofa should back against a wall for "support" and not turn its back to the door. The wealth corner (usually diagonal from the main door) can hold a wealth bowl or money-drawing plants.
- Plants: indoor evergreens, money trees, and golden pothos are believed to draw luck and vitality; thorny plants like cacti are considered unsuitable indoors.

【Feng Shui Objects and Deflection Tools】
- Bagua mirror: hung above a doorway to reflect harmful energy. A convex mirror deflects a road clash; a concave one draws in good energy.
- Shigandang: a stone tablet set at a road junction or alley corner to suppress harmful energy, most often carved with "Mount Tai Shigandang."
- Wind Lion God (Fengshiye): the most iconic feng shui object of Kinmen, used to subdue the wind and ward off evil.
- Pixiu: a mythical beast that only takes in and never lets out, symbolizing the drawing in and holding of wealth -- often displayed in shops and offices.
- Five Emperor Coins: copper coins from five Qing emperors (Shunzhi, Kangxi, Yongzheng, Qianlong, Jiaqing), strung together and hung on a door or set beneath a threshold to deflect harm and draw wealth.
- Shanhai Zhen: a wooden plaque bearing a landscape and taiji diagram, hung above a doorway or facing the source of harmful energy -- the most common home deflection tool in Taiwan.

【Feng Shui Today】
Modern Taiwanese hold every kind of view on feng shui: some believe wholeheartedly and won't buy a property without a master's inspection; some treat it as a reference without being rigid; others see it as psychological comfort. Whatever the degree of belief, feng shui has long since woven itself into Taiwanese architecture, interior design, and urban planning -- even new housing developments market their "feng shui layout" as a selling point, proof that this culture still carries real weight today.

title: Spirit Mediums (Jitong) and Oracles
summary: At a temple procession, the man who suddenly shakes all over, seizes a shark-tooth sword and strikes his own forehead without flinching, is a jitong -- a spirit medium, the deity's chosen mouthpiece on earth. By "entering trance," he lets the deity possess his body to pass on divine messages, heal the sick, dispel misfortune, and point the lost toward a way through.
content:
In the midst of a temple procession, a man begins to shake violently. His gaze shifts, he takes up a shark-tooth sword and brings it down on his own forehead -- blood runs, yet he seems to feel no pain. That is no longer him, the onlookers say; a deity has "descended." This man is a jitong (also called tongji or lingji), the spirit medium believed to be the deity's spokesperson in the human world.

【What Is a Jitong?】
"Ji" means the medium through which a spirit descends; "tong" means pure and undefiled. A jitong is a mortal chosen by a deity to speak for it -- of any gender or age. The choosing is usually not voluntary: the person may suddenly tremble for no reason, speak in strange words, or dream again and again of a particular deity summoning them. Once a temple ritual master confirms it, they are recognized as "taken" by that deity. Then comes a period of "training the medium" (xun ji), learning to receive the deity's descent steadily.

【Entering Trance】
The trance usually takes place on specific occasions -- a deity's birthday, a temple procession, or a consultation session. The ritual master opens the rite with chanting, bell-ringing, and incense, and under his guidance the medium slowly slips into a trance. Once in it, the medium's words and acts are believed to be no longer his own but the deity's: the voice changes, the expression turns stern or compassionate, and the speech may shift into classical Chinese or an old dialect.

【Wielding the Five Treasures (Cao Wu Bao)】
The most striking thing about a Taiwanese jitong is "wielding the five treasures" -- using ritual weapons to wound himself while in trance:
- Seven Star Sword: a short sword struck against the back or chest.
- Shark Sword (shark-tooth club): a weapon of shark teeth struck against the forehead or back, drawing blood, though the medium is said to feel no pain.
- Bronze Rod: a bronze staff struck against the body.
- Spiked Ball (wolf-tooth mace): a ball studded with iron spikes, struck against the whole body.
- Moon Axe: an axe-shaped implement struck with its flat face.
The practice is believed to purify the implements or consecrate talismans with the medium's blood, and to display the deity's power. Not every jitong does this, though -- those who convey the deity's message by speech alone are called "wen ji" (civil mediums), while those who wield the five treasures are "wu ji" (martial mediums).

【The Interpreter (Zhuotou)】
When the deity descends, its words are often obscure -- classical Chinese, a local dialect, or a garbled mutter -- so a "zhuotou" (interpreter, also called translator or jijiao) stands by to render them. Usually a seasoned old devotee or ritual master, the interpreter can decode the medium's speech and gestures and turn the deity's message into modern words worshippers can follow. The role is crucial: a good interpreter makes the whole consultation flow and ring true.

【The Consultation】
To consult the jitong, a worshipper usually first offers incense and casts divination blocks to confirm the deity is willing, then waits their turn. The questions range widely: health, marriage and relationships, career and money, home feng shui, a child's schooling, and more. Through the interpreter, the jitong gives specific advice, and may prescribe a "medicine poem" (a remedy built mainly of Chinese herbal ingredients) or direct the worshipper to undergo certain rites, such as jigai or Tai Sui pacification.

【Social Role and Controversy】
The jitong's place in Taiwanese society is complex and subtle. To devout believers he is the deity's compassion made flesh, a vital outlet for comfort and life guidance; critics worry that some mediums exploit worshippers' trust for private gain. In recent years the culture has been shifting -- some temples have built more transparent consultation systems, and scholars have begun studying trance from anthropological and psychological angles. Whichever side one takes, jitong culture is one strand of Taiwanese folk religion, carrying centuries of historical memory and folk wisdom.

title: Taoist Priests and Ritual Masters
summary: They both wear Taoist robes, but a "daoshi" (Taoist priest) and a "fashi" (ritual master) are not the same thing. Through long years of cultivation and master-to-disciple transmission, they command the liturgical arts, carrying the weight at temple festivals, life-cycle rituals, and rites for blessing and calamity -- the professional intermediaries between the human and divine worlds.
content:
At a jiao festival you may see two kinds of men in Taoist robes: one presiding over a solemn grand liturgy, the other with a red band around his head calming a frightened soul. Taiwanese often lump them together as "shigong," but strictly speaking a daoshi (Taoist priest) and a fashi (ritual master) are not the same. Both have passed through long years of cultivation and master-disciple transmission, and both serve as professional intermediaries between the human and spirit worlds.

【Priest or Ritual Master?】
In Taiwan the two terms are often used interchangeably, but strictly there are distinctions:
- Taoist priest (daoshi, also daozhang or daogong): belongs to the Zhengyi (Orthodox Unity) tradition, has undergone a formal "ordination" (a ceremony akin to receiving religious credentials), and holds a documented master-disciple lineage. Their liturgies are more rigorous, grounded in Taoist scripture and centered on communion with the Three Pure Ones; they usually preside over major jiao rituals, peace assemblies, and other formal occasions.
- Ritual master (fashi, also "red-cap master" or "black-cap master"): a practitioner who blends Taoist, Buddhist, and folk elements. The "red-cap master" wears a red headband and handles mainly blessing rites (shoujing, jigai, Tai Sui pacification); the "black-cap master" wears a black headband and handles mainly funerary and salvation rites. Their ceremonies are more flexible and take in more local folk elements.
- Shijiao ritual master: a practitioner who works mainly from Buddhist scripture but folds in Taoist liturgy, especially common in southern Taiwan.

【Training and Transmission】
Becoming a priest or ritual master means enduring a long apprenticeship. Tradition follows the master-disciple system: after being taken into a lineage, the disciple starts with the humblest tasks -- carrying implements, setting up the altar -- then learns chanting, ritual pacing, visualization, talisman-writing, and the use of the implements, step by step. Full training usually takes three to five years or more, with the master passing on different levels of art according to the disciple's aptitude and insight. At a certain point, the disciple must travel to a Taoist holy site (such as Tainan's Altar of Heaven or Taipei's Zhinan Temple) for the "ordination" or "transmission" ceremony that grants formal religious standing.

In Taiwan the priesthood is often hereditary -- father to son, son to grandson -- forming what are called "ritual altar families." Tainan has the densest concentration of them, many having carried their lineages for more than ten generations, all the way back to the Qing dynasty. These families pass down not only their liturgical craft but also large collections of precious hand-copied scriptures and old ritual implements.

【Implements and Equipment】
Each implement a priest uses carries its own symbolism:
- Emperor Bell (Sanqing Bell): shaken to summon the Three Pure Ones and all the celestial deities down to the altar.
- Command Flags: the authority of the heavenly court, in five colors (green, red, yellow, white, black) for the five directions; a wave of the flags issues divine orders.
- Dragon Horn: made from ox horn or a conch shell, its deep note intimidates evil spirits and signals the heavenly court.
- Treasure Sword (Seven Star Sword): a ritual sword patterned with the Big Dipper, for slaying demons and consecrating sacred objects.
- Court Tablet (hand board): a ceremonial board held when paying respect to the Celestial Worthies, a token of reverence.
- Tianpeng Ruler (Thunder Token): a ritual ruler of lightning-struck wood, struck to sound with demon-warding, spirit-subduing effect.

【Vestments】
A priest wears different robes for different occasions:
- Red robe: for blessing rites, jiao rituals, and other auspicious occasions.
- Black or dark-blue robe: for salvation and funerary rites.
- Nine Palace Bagua robe: an ornate robe embroidered with the eight trigrams, reserved for the highest-grade liturgies.
- Plain robe (zhuangyi): a simple everyday Taoist garment.
The head wears a "yellow crown" or a "net cap," and the feet, "cloud shoes" stitched with cloud patterns.

【Their Role in Taiwanese Society】
Priests and ritual masters wear many hats in Taiwan: presiders at temple festivals, officiants of life-cycle rites (from a child's "courage-building" ceremony to an elder's funerary merit rites), spiritual counselors to their communities, and guardians of traditional culture. As times change, some younger priests have begun sharing liturgical knowledge on social media, and academic bodies (such as National Chengchi University's Institute for the Study of Religion) have partnered with ritual altars for fieldwork and digital archiving, setting down a record of this precious religious heritage.

title: Common Mantras, Scriptures, and Prayers
summary: "Namo Amitabha Buddha," "Om Mani Padme Hum," "Execute forthwith as decreed" -- these are sounds you have surely heard. From the Buddhist chanting of mantras and the Buddha's name to Taoist scripture recitation and prayer, these sacred words carry thousands of years of religious wisdom and remain the daily practice of countless believers.
content:
"Amitabha" as a greeting, "Amitabha" blurted out after a fright, and the Taoist priest in every film who ends with a cry of "Execute forthwith as decreed" -- these sounds long ago worked their way into everyday Taiwanese life. Mantras and scriptures, whether the Buddhist chanting of mantras and the Buddha's name, the Taoist recitation of scripture and prayer, or the incantations of folk religion, all carry thousands of years of religious wisdom, and remain a core daily practice for countless believers.

【Namo Amitabha Buddha】
"Namo Amitabha Buddha" (Namo Amitabhaya Buddhaya) is probably the most universally known Buddha-name in Taiwan -- almost everyone can chant it. "Namo" means to take refuge in, to pay homage; "Amitabha" means Infinite Light and Infinite Life. Pure Land Buddhism holds that by whole-heartedly reciting this six-syllable name, one will be met and guided by Amitabha Buddha at the moment of death to rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. In Taiwan the phrase has long slipped its religious frame: said in greeting it's a blessing, said after a scare it's a plea for peace, and said often enough it becomes a simple figure of speech.

【The Great Compassion Mantra (Dabeizhou)】
The Great Compassion Mantra -- in full, "The Great Compassion Heart Dharani of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva" -- runs to 84 lines and is the long mantra Taiwanese Buddhists recite most. Spoken by Avalokitesvara (Guanyin), its recitation brings the bodhisattva's blessing and protection, easing sickness, warding off disaster, and deepening wisdom. Many Buddhists make it a daily practice, chanting it seven or twenty-one times, and temples recite it in their morning and evening services. Even "Great Compassion Water" -- water blessed with the mantra -- is believed to hold a marvelous power to heal and dispel calamity.

【The Heart Sutra (Bore Boluomiduo Xinjing)】
The Heart Sutra, at just 260 characters, is regarded as the distilled essence of the entire 600-volume Great Prajna Sutra, and is the scripture Taiwanese Buddhists know best. Its core -- "Form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form; form is emptiness, emptiness is form" -- voices the Buddhist wisdom of "emptiness" (sunyata), while its closing line, "Gate gate paragate parasamgate bodhi svaha," is the summation mantra of the whole sutra. The Heart Sutra is widely copied ("sutra-copying" is a common practice among Taiwanese Buddhists), memorized, and chanted, and is a favorite subject for calligraphers.

【The Rebirth Mantra (Wangsheng Zhou)】
The Rebirth Mantra -- in full, "The Dharani for Pulling Out the Root of All Karmic Obstacles and Gaining Rebirth in the Pure Land" -- is one of the most familiar sounds in Taiwanese funeral custom. At memorial services, dharma assemblies, and in private practice, it is recited for the departed, praying that their karmic obstacles dissolve and they are reborn in the Western Pure Land. Many Taiwanese, even those who aren't devout Buddhists, will chant a passage of it after a loved one passes, as an offering of remembrance.

【The Six-Syllable Mantra (Om Mani Padme Hum)】
Om Mani Padme Hum is the heart mantra of Avalokitesvara, also known as the "Six-Syllable Great Bright Mantra." Each syllable stands for one of the bodhisattva's compassionate vows, and to recite it is to receive Avalokitesvara's protection. In Taiwan many Buddhists chant it while turning a prayer wheel or telling mala beads -- a practice for anytime, anywhere.

【Execute Forthwith as Decreed by Taishang Laojun】
This is the most common closing formula in Taoist rites, appearing at the end of nearly every talismanic command and incantation. "Taishang Laojun" is one of the highest deities in Taoism (identified with Laozi), and "ji ji ru lu ling" means "execute at once, as by force of law." To utter it is for the priest to issue orders on Taishang Laojun's authority, commanding ghosts and spirits to obey. In folk culture the line is all but synonymous with Taoism, and the Taoist characters of film and television are forever delivering it.

【The Mouth- and Body-Purifying Incantations】
Before performing a rite or reciting scripture, a Taoist practitioner first recites the "Mouth-Purifying Incantation" and "Body-Purifying Incantation" to cleanse body and mind. The first keeps the mouth clean, so that impure speech-karma won't rob the recitation of its power; the second cleanses the whole energy field, so one faces the deities in the purest state. These two are basic daily practice for a priest and an essential preparation before opening the altar.

【The Medicine Buddha Mantra】
The Medicine Buddha Mantra -- in full, "The Consecration Mantra of the Medicine Master of Lapis Lazuli Light Tathagata" -- is recited to pray for health and to cure illness. In Taiwan many worshippers chant it when they or their loved ones fall ill, then light a "Medicine Buddha Lamp" before the Medicine Buddha to pray for recovery. Some temples regularly hold a "Medicine Buddha Dharma Assembly" to chant the Medicine Buddha's sutra and mantra together.

【Common Folk Prayer Formulas】
Beyond the formal mantras and scriptures, folk religion also keeps many prayer formulas handed down over generations. The most basic is the self-introduction you use when worshipping at a temple: "Your disciple [name], living at [address], born on the [lunar date], comes today with a sincere heart to pray for [request], hoping that [desired outcome]..." Reporting yourself clearly is the basic courtesy of making yourself known to the deity. "Spirits of heaven, spirits of earth" is a common opening line in fright-calming, while "Execute forthwith as decreed -- dismissed!" is a simplified version of the Taoist formula, widely used among ordinary folk.

title: Red Envelopes (Hongbao)
summary: The money inside a Lunar New Year red envelope is called yasui qian, literally "money that presses down the sui" - a demon said to touch sleeping children on New Year's Eve. Amounts must be even, never contain a four, and the envelope is never reused.
content:
The reunion dinner is winding down when an elder stands up and reaches into a pocket. Every child at the table goes quiet. This is the moment.

[What the money is pressing down]
The formal name for the money in a red envelope is yasui qian. The common folk explanation is that sui here originally meant a demon, not a year - a creature said to stroke the foreheads of sleeping children on New Year's Eve, leaving them feverish and delirious. One family wrapped eight copper coins in red paper and left them by their child's pillow. The demon came close, the coins caught the light, and it fled.

Early yasui qian really were copper coins, threaded on red string. A hundred coins on one string was called a hundred-year string, a wish for a long life. Paper money replaced the coins, and the string became the envelope.

[Rules about the amount]
- Always an even number: NT$600, 1,200, 2,000 and 3,600 are all common. Odd amounts belong in white envelopes, which are for funerals.
- Never a four: NT$400 or 4,000 is out, because "four" sounds like "death" in both Mandarin and Taiwanese.
- Six and eight are favoured: six for things going smoothly, eight for wealth.
- Envelopes given upward to parents run larger. That one is called tiansui, "adding a year" - a wish that they gain another one.

[When to give]
Strictly speaking, after the New Year's Eve vigil, so the money accompanies the child across the turn of the year. In practice most families hand them out right after dinner. Some households make children sleep with the envelope under the pillow before opening it, which is the literal version of pressing down the year.

[Taboos still observed]
- Never reuse an envelope. A used one carries last year with it.
- Never open one and reseal it.
- Never open it in front of the giver. Counting the money in front of them is rude; wait until you have left the room.
- Traditionally only married people give. Unmarried adults receive, no matter their age.

[Who gives to whom]
Downward to children, upward to parents and elders. Sideways, between peers, is unusual. Some households also give to a helper, a driver, or the building's caretaker, which is closer to a tip and has no fixed amount.

[The envelope today]
Digital transfers through LINE Pay or JKOPay are now ordinary. The paper envelope has not gone away, though, because the point was never the money. It is the act of putting something into someone's hands. That is also why the queue at the bank for crisp new notes still forms every year in the last week before the holiday.

title: Spring Couplets (Chunlian)
summary: Before red paper, the couplets flanking a Taiwanese doorway were two peach-wood boards painted with the door gods Shentu and Yulei. The paper replaced the wood; the rules stayed - facing the door, the first line goes on the right, and the header reads right to left.
content:
On the afternoon of New Year's Eve the whole lane fills with the sound of paper tearing. Last year's couplets have to come down before the new ones go up. The year starts with that gesture.

[From peach wood to red paper]
Spring couplets began as taofu - two peach-wood boards hung on either side of a door, bearing the names of Shentu and Yulei, the two door gods. Peach wood was believed to repel evil, and the gods kept unclean things out. Red paper with auspicious lines eventually took their place. When Wang Anshi wrote about replacing the old charms with new peaches, this is the swap he meant.

[How to hang them]
This is where most people get it wrong:
- The first line goes on the right, the second on the left, as you face the door from outside rather than standing inside it.
- Telling the lines apart: listen to the last character. The first line ends on a falling tone, the second on a level tone.
- The horizontal header is written right to left, which is why the first line belongs on the right.
- The upside-down fu character is contested. On a main door, tradition says do not invert it; an inverted fu belongs on a rice bin or a cupboard. Inverted on the front door, it reads as good fortune tipping over before it gets inside.

[Where they go]
- Both sides of the main door: the couplet proper.
- Above the lintel: the header.
- Centre of the door panel: a single fu or chun character.
- Rice bin, refrigerator, car: smaller slips reading full, spring, or prosper.
- Kitchen: often a line about the five flavours in harmony.

[When to hang and when to remove]
New Year's Eve is the usual day, though some hang them the evening before. Avoid leaving it until after dark; folk practice holds that couplets hung at night do not hold. Whatever comes down is replaced the same day, so the doorway is never left bare overnight.

Taking them down varies by region. Some places wait for the Lantern Festival, others leave them until they fall apart on their own. Most Taiwanese households simply strip the old ones the following New Year's Eve, which means the couplet hangs for a full year.

[Why anyone still bothers]
Printed couplets took over long ago and hang in rows in every supermarket by December. Yet people still queue in front of calligraphers before the holiday, because what goes on that paper is what the household wants this year. A shop asks for wealth. A family with a child sitting exams asks for a place on the list. Someone who has just moved in asks for a settled home. The two lines by the door are a set of resolutions, written large enough for the neighbours to read.
